intro: A call to prayer rises from a mosque in Bridgeview. A family in Rogers Park breaks the Ramadan fast with a date and a glass of water. A student in Indonesia recites the same Arabic verses as a student in Chicago. About two billion people today call themselves Muslims, and Islam is one of the largest religions in the world.

This unit studies Islam the way a historian does. First you will follow Muhammad's life as Muslims tell it, learn how the Qur'an is organized and recited, and see the Five Pillars in daily life. Then you will trace how Muslim states, scholars and traders linked Spain, West Africa, Baghdad, India and Indonesia, and how Muslims came to America.

By the end, you will be able to explain key Muslim beliefs and practices in their own terms, describe the Sunni and Shia branches, place major events on a timeline, and use real sources, from the Qur'an to a traveler's diary, to support what you say.
bigQuestion: How did a message Muslims say began in a cave near Mecca shape a faith, a community and a civilization that reaches around the world?

test.q: Where do Muslims say the first revelation came to Muhammad?
choices: In the cave of Hira near Mecca
In the Great Mosque of Damascus
test.why: Muslim tradition places the first revelation in the cave of Hira, c. 610.

choices: The hijra took place, and the Islamic calendar counts from it
The Qur'an was translated into Latin
test.why: The hijra to Medina in 622 is year one of the Islamic calendar.

test.q: Which of these is NOT one of the Five Pillars?
test.why: The pillars are shahada, salat, zakat, sawm and hajj; a minaret is part of a mosque building.

test.q: What does the Arabic word Qur'an mean?
Which statement about Sunni and Shia Muslims is accurate?
choices: They split first over who should lead after Muhammad
Only Sunni Muslims fast in Ramadan
Shia Muslims use a different Qur'an
Sunni Muslims do not make the hajj
test.why: The two branches share the Qur'an and pillars; the split began over leadership.
The Sunnah is Muhammad's example, known through hadith reports.
The Abbasids founded Baghdad in 762 and ruled from it.

test.q: What did scholars at the House of Wisdom mainly do?
choices: Translated and studied books from many languages
test.why: Baghdad's scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic.

test.q: Which city in Spain had a Great Mosque begun in 785?
test.why: Work on Córdoba's Great Mosque began in 785.
Mansa Musa ruled Mali and made the hajj in 1324.

test.q: Why does Ramadan move through the seasons?
choices: The Islamic calendar is lunar and about 11 days shorter than the solar year
Each country picks its own month
It was moved by the Ottomans
test.why: The lunar year is about 354 days, so Ramadan shifts earlier each year.

test.q: What do pilgrims remember when they walk between two hills on hajj?
choices: Hagar searching for water for Ishmael
test.why: The walk recalls Hagar's search for water.

test.q: Which country has the largest Muslim population?
test.why: Indonesia has more Muslims than any other country.

test.q: Why is Omar ibn Said important to American history?
choices: He led the Nation of Islam
He was an enslaved Muslim who wrote his life story in Arabic
test.why: His 1831 Arabic autobiography shows Muslims were in America during slavery.

test.q: A historian says, "Muslim rule spread quickly, but conversion was slow." What does this mean?
choices: Many people kept their own faith for generations under Muslim rulers
Muslim rulers never governed other lands
test.why: Historians describe conversion in conquered lands as taking centuries.

write.prompt: Why did learning matter so much in Islamic civilization? Use two or three sources from this unit, such as Surah 96, Surah 20:114, al-Khwarizmi's preface or Ibn Battuta's account of Mali, and explain what each shows about how Muslims have valued knowledge.
tips: Name each source you cite, with its surah and verse or its author and date.
Attribute beliefs: write "Muslims believe" or "according to the Qur'an."
Use at least three terms from the unit, such as surah, caliph or House of Wisdom.
Explain, do not judge: say what the source shows and why it matters.
